name.scientific: Cajamarca department box, first download (mixed coast and Andes)

why.simple: Air in the Andes mountains has been getting warmer for many years.
why.scientific: Mean annual temperature in the tropical Andes rose by 0.10-0.11 °C per decade over 1939-1998 and faster (0.32-0.34 °C per decade) over the last 25 years of that series; significant at 95% even at the highest elevations. This is a surface-station record for 1939-1998, so it motivates the sign, not the 2002+ rate. Source: Vuille, M. and Bradley, R. S., Mean annual temperature trends and their vertical structure in the tropical Andes, Geophysical Research Letters 27(23), 2000. https://doi.org/10.1029/2000GL011871

text.simple: Another instrument shows the same direction, but is not sure yet.
text.scientific: Overlapping window 2002-09 to 2021-12, same place, each series de-seasonalised over that window. AIRS (Surface air temperature (night-time, AIRS descending)): +0.218 °C per decade, p = 0.0002. MERRA-2 (2-m air temperature (NASA POWER, MERRA-2-based)): +0.05 °C per decade, p = 0.838 (p is the weaker of the two decisive tests). Same sign, but only one is significant at 0.05. AIRS is a snapshot at about 1:30 (day or night pass), the other series is a daily mean: compare the direction only, not the size. The grid cells differ (1.0° vs 0.5°), so the footprints differ.

why.simple: This record can only spot changes bigger than a typical one.
why.scientific: MDT ≈ 0.23 °C/decade over 19.3 yr vs expected 0.20 (Vuille, M. and Bradley, R. S., Mean annual temperature trends and their vertical structure in the tropical Andes, Geophysical Research Letters 27(23), 2000. https://doi.org/10.1029/2000GL011871): not detectable.

text.simple: The two instruments do not tell the same story yet.
text.scientific: Overlapping window 2002-09 to 2021-12, same place, each series de-seasonalised over that window. AIRS (Surface air temperature (daytime, AIRS ascending)): -0.466 °C per decade, p = 1.42e-07. MERRA-2 (2-m air temperature (NASA POWER, MERRA-2-based)): +0.05 °C per decade, p = 0.838 (p is the weaker of the two decisive tests). Neither is significant at 0.05 together with the same sign, so there is no contrast to report. AIRS is a snapshot at about 1:30 (day or night pass), the other series is a daily mean: compare the direction only, not the size. The grid cells differ (1.0° vs 0.5°), so the footprints differ.

text.simple: Your place is dry and hot. It is high up above the sea. Most rain comes from January to April. This is a computer model estimate.
text.scientific: Köppen–Geiger BSh (Beck et al. 2018 rules on NASA POWER 1981–2025 climatology, MERRA-2 based); IPCC AR6 region NWS (N.W.South-America); model-grid elevation 1566 m (high up: 1500 m or more); wet months January to April, dry months June to August (long-term monthly means).
